title: Milestone: Myth and City
objective: After this level you can connect Greek myths, gods and city-states into one picture.
summary: With no sacred books, Greeks learned their gods from poets like Homer and Hesiod, and their cities claimed heroes: Theseus for Athens, Perseus for Mycenae.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Greek myths weren’t set in never-never land.
cards.body: The gods had a real mountain, and the heroes had real hometowns. Let’s see how myth and city fit together.

cards.headline: Poets wrote the gods’ biography
cards.body: Greek religion had no sacred books. So who told Greeks what their gods were like? Herodotus had an answer: Homer and Hesiod, who he supposed lived no more than 400 years before him. They taught the Greeks the gods’ family tree, gave the gods their names, set their jobs and described their looks. Level 6 called Homer Greece’s textbook. For the gods, he was the encyclopedia too.

cards.headline: A legend on the city calendar
cards.body: The historian Thucydides wrote that before Theseus, Attica was a patchwork of independent towns, each with its own council. Theseus, he said, merged them into one council at Athens, and the Athenians kept a state-funded Feast of Union, the Synoecia, dating from him. A hero who fought a monster in a maze was also remembered as the man who made Athens one city.

questions.prompt: Gods and Heroes recap: when Zeus and his brothers drew lots, what did Hades get?

options.label: Mount Olympus
options.rationale: The lots split sky, sea and underworld.

questions.explanation: Zeus drew the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld.

questions.prompt: Herodotus said Homer helped shape the Greek gods. What role did Level 6 say Homer’s epics played in Greek life?

options.label: They were the basis of Greek education
They were read aloud only by priests
options.rationale: They were at the heart of education.

options.label: They were banned in the Classical age
options.rationale: They were at the heart of it.

options.label: They were the written law of Athens

questions.explanation: Homer’s epics were the basis of Greek education and culture, and Herodotus credited Homer and Hesiod with the gods’ names and forms.

questions.prompt: Myth and City recap: whose skin did Heracles wear after his first labor?

options.label: The Hydra’s
options.rationale: The Hydra was the second labor.

options.label: Cerberus’s
options.rationale: Cerberus went back to the underworld.

questions.explanation: His first labor was killing the Nemean lion, whose skin he wore ever after.

questions.prompt: According to Herodotus, what did Homer and Hesiod give the Greeks?

options.label: Their first written laws
options.rationale: Herodotus credited them with the gods.

options.label: The gods’ names, roles, looks and family tree
Their first stone temples
options.rationale: He credited them with ideas, not buildings.

questions.explanation: Herodotus wrote that Homer and Hesiod taught the Greeks the gods’ descent, gave them names, set their spheres and described their forms.

questions.prompt: Why did the Athenians hold their Feast of Union in honor of Theseus?

options.label: He had drawn the sea by lot
He had killed Poseidon’s son
options.rationale: That was Odysseus’s deed, against Polyphemus.

options.label: Thucydides credited him with merging Attica’s towns under Athens

questions.explanation: Thucydides wrote that Theseus merged Attica’s town councils into one at Athens, and the Synoecia dated from him.

questions.prompt: Two heroes are tied to Level 4’s Mycenaean strongholds. Which pairing is right?

options.label: Theseus founded Mycenae; Perseus served at Tiryns
Heracles founded Mycenae; Theseus ruled Tiryns
Odysseus founded Mycenae; Heracles ruled Tiryns
Perseus founded Mycenae; Heracles served at Tiryns

questions.explanation: Perseus was said to have founded Mycenae, and Heracles served Eurystheus in Tiryns: both Mycenaean strongholds.

questions.prompt: Gods and Heroes recap: which goddess ended up wearing Medusa’s head on her aegis?

options.label: Hera, queen of the gods
options.rationale: It went to the goddess of strategy.

options.label: Athena, goddess of war and practical reason
Demeter, goddess of grain
options.rationale: Demeter had no part in it.

questions.explanation: Medusa’s head was given to Athena, who placed it on her aegis; she had helped Perseus with the shield.
